title: Dynamic Updates in the Domain Name System (DNS UPDATE)
summary: This standards-track specification defines the DNS UPDATE opcode, which lets a client add or delete records in a zone while the server runs. Updates can depend on prerequisites, such as whether a record set already exists.

eli5.summary: Instead of rewriting the whole phone book, you can add or cross out one entry, but only if certain conditions are true.

questions: how to add records to a dns zone dynamically
how does dynamic dns update work
subtitle: How to add and delete DNS records in a live zone with a single, conditional, all-or-nothing message.

tldr.problem: DNS was designed for a statically configured database, where every change was an external edit to a zone's Master File.
tldr.mechanism: A new UPDATE opcode carries a zone, a list of prerequisites and a list of records to add or delete. The primary master applies the update only if every prerequisite holds.
tldr.outcome: UPDATE is atomic, but without extra security anyone who can reach an authoritative server could alter its zones, so the RFC strongly recommends using it only with RFC 2137 or equivalent protection.

sections.title: Dynamic Updates and Server Roles
sections.content:
The Domain Name System was originally designed to support queries of a statically configured database. Data was expected to change only rarely, and all updates were external edits to a zone's Master File. DNS UPDATE adds an opcode that can add or delete resource records (RRs) or RRsets in a given zone while it is being served.

The RFC also sharpens the server roles from RFC 1035 and RFC 1996. A slave retrieves the zone by AXFR or IXFR. A master is a source of that data. The primary master sits at the root of the transfer dependency graph, is named in the SOA MNAME field, and there is exactly one per zone. Only the primary master actually modifies the zone.

Comparison rules matter: two RRs are equal if NAME, CLASS, TYPE, RDLENGTH and RDATA match, and the TTL is excluded. Wildcarding and aliasing are disabled, so a wildcard only matches a wildcard, and a CNAME is never followed.
sections.eli5: A phone book used to be reprinted whenever something changed. This lets one person, the head clerk, change a single line while people keep using the book.

sections.title: The UPDATE Message
sections.content:
An UPDATE message reuses the DNS message layout with five parts: a Header, a Zone section naming the zone to update, a Prerequisite section of records that must (or must not) pre-exist, an Update section of records to add or delete, and an Additional Data section. The header's four count fields are renamed ZOCOUNT, PRCOUNT, UPCOUNT and ADCOUNT. The opcode value for UPDATE is 5, and UPDATE uses only the QR flag bit. It may travel in a UDP datagram, if it fits, or over TCP.

The Zone section must contain exactly one record, whose ZTYPE is SOA. The RFC overloads the CLASS field: ANY and NONE act as markers that change what a record means, which works because every record in the message belongs to one zone.

New response codes cover update failures: YXDOMAIN (6), YXRRSET (7), NXRRSET (8), NOTAUTH (9) and NOTZONE (10). CLASS NONE is 254.
sections.eli5: The note has parts: which book, what must be true first, and what to write or cross out. Special words in the note mark which is which.

sections.title: Prerequisites, Updates and Server Processing
sections.content:
A server first checks the Zone section: it answers NOTIMP if it does not implement the opcode, FORMERR if there is not exactly one SOA record, and NOTAUTH if it is not authoritative for the zone. A slave forwards the request toward the primary master. The primary master then evaluates five kinds of prerequisite: an RRset exists (value independent), an RRset exists (value dependent), an RRset does not exist, a name is in use, or a name is not in use.

If prerequisites pass and the requestor is permitted (otherwise the server may answer REFUSED), the Update section is processed in order. The four operations are: add to an RRset, delete an RRset, delete all RRsets from a name, and delete one RR from an RRset. Duplicate additions are silently ignored, and deletes of things that do not exist are ignored too. At the zone apex, SOA and NS records are protected: the last NS RR cannot be deleted, and an SOA with a lower or equal serial is ignored.

UPDATE is atomic. If any prerequisite fails, no update operation takes place. The server must also commit the change to nonvolatile storage before responding or answering queries for the modified zone, and concurrent transactions that depend on each other must be serialized.

If the zone's SOA serial is not changed by the update, the server increments it automatically. One suggested trigger is a configurable number of updates since the last change, defaulting to one hundred (100). The serial must only move in a positive direction and must never be zero.
sections.eli5: The clerk first checks that you asked the right office and that your conditions are true. Only then does the clerk make every change on your list, and writes it down permanently before telling anyone.

sections.title: Requestors, Duplicates and Forwarding
sections.content:
A requestor needs to know the zone name and find its name servers. It should try the primary master first when it is reachable, and moves to the next server if it gets SERVFAIL, NOTIMP, no response in time, or an ICMP port-unreachable. Any other RCODE is returned to the caller.

Messages can arrive zero, one or several times and out of order, which includes the case of a malicious replay. The RFC's remedy is a marker RR: the update deletes the old marker and adds a new one with different data, and a prerequisite requires the old marker to be present. A duplicate then fails, because only the first finds the old marker. The zone's SOA RR is an obvious choice, and the same trick supports an atomic read-modify-write cycle.

Because a lost UDP response can make a successful update look like a failure when a retry fails its prerequisites, requestors who need an accurate response code must use TCP. A forwarding slave allocates a new ID, forwards toward the servers it would use for AXFR or IXFR, must use TCP if the original requestor did, and does not answer until the forward server does.
sections.eli5: If your note might be photocopied and delivered twice, you add a rule such as "only do this if page 7 still has the old stamp". The second copy fails because the stamp has changed.

sections.title: Design Notes and Corner Cases
sections.content:
Section 7 is explicitly not part of the formal specification. It records design reasoning. Data-present and data-absent conditions belong in the Prerequisite section, because the Update section itself cannot raise such errors. The Additional Data section can carry out-of-zone glue, which servers may use or ignore.

Several limits are spelled out. A zone cannot be created with this protocol, so adding or deleting SOA records is unsupported. Without a secure update protocol, servers are expected to accept updates only from statically configured source addresses, with DHCP servers named as likely candidates. All TTLs in an RRset should be the same. The primary master does no semantic checking on added RRs. The forwarding scheme forbids loops in the AXFR dependency graph, since UPDATE forwarding has no loop detection.
sections.eli5: This part is the author's notes on why the rules look the way they do, plus a list of odd cases to watch out for.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Without RFC 2137 or equivalent technology, anyone who can reach an authoritative name server could alter the contents of any zone on it. The RFC calls this a serious increase in vulnerability and very strongly recommends not using the protocol without RFC 2137 or other equivalently strong measures such as IPsec.

There is also a denial-of-service risk. Flooding an update forwarder with TCP sessions that the primary master will refuse for permission reasons ties up the forwarder's synchronous TCP sessions. The connection management of RFC 1035 limits large-scale damage but cannot prevent some queries going unanswered during the attack.
sections.eli5: If anyone could hand the clerk a note, anyone could change the book. So the rules say to check who is allowed, and never to skip that check.

items.label: UPDATE
items.desc: Marks the message as a dynamic update.

items.label: NONE
items.desc: Marker class used in prerequisites and deletes.

items.label: YXDOMAIN
items.desc: Some name that ought not to exist, does exist.

items.label: YXRRSET
items.desc: Some RRset that ought not to exist, does exist.

items.label: NXRRSET
items.desc: Some RRset that ought to exist, does not exist.

items.label: NOTAUTH
items.desc: The server is not authoritative for the zone named in the Zone Section.

items.label: NOTZONE
items.desc: A name in the Prerequisite or Update Section is not within the zone.
